paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients, where only whole-number answers count. The linear kind adds up several unknowns, each multiplied by a fixed number, and sets that total equal to a constant. With two unknowns it is written ax + by = c, where a, b and c are integers you are given, and you look for integers x and y.

paragraphs.heading: Named after Diophantus
paragraphs.text: The name honours Diophantus of Alexandria, a Hellenistic mathematician of the 3rd century who studied equations like these. He was also one of the first mathematicians to use symbols in algebra. The study of such whole-number problems that he started is now called Diophantine analysis.

paragraphs.heading: When a solution exists
paragraphs.text: Whether ax + by = c has any solution at all depends on a single number, d = gcd (a, b), the greatest common divisor of a and b. A solution exists exactly when d divides c, written d∣c. If d does not divide c, no choice of integers x and y will work.

paragraphs.heading: Finding every solution
paragraphs.text: Once you have one solution, call it x₀, y₀, you can produce all the rest. Take x = x₀ + (b/d)t and y = y₀ − (a/d)t, and let t be any integer you like. Every other solution has this shape, and since t can be any integer, there are infinitely many of them.

paragraphs.heading: Many equations at once
paragraphs.text: A whole system of these equations can be packed into matrix form as AX = C. Here A is an m × n table of integers, X is a column of n unknowns, and C is a column of m integers. Any such system can be solved by working out its matrix's Smith normal form, much like the reduced row echelon form is used for ordinary linear equations over a field. The Hermite normal form works as well, though it does not give the solutions directly: several linear equations then have to be solved one after another. Richard Zippel argued that the triangular Hermite form is all you need, and that it is much easier to compute than the diagonal Smith form.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs.text: These equations sit at the base of integer linear programming. That field looks for whole-number solutions to linear systems that also contain inequalities, picking ones that are best in some sense. For that reason, textbooks on integer programming usually include a treatment of systems of linear Diophantine equations.
